University of Washington, Seattle, USA (single author)
Proposes an approach (ContextCov: compiles agent instruction files such as AGENTS.md into executable guardrails) and compares it with two baselines (Vanilla, LLM Reflection) on SWE-bench Lite
ContextCov (no version; code at github.com/reSHARMA/ContextCov). Input artefact: Agent Instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, copilot-instructions.md)

Input: agent instruction file (Markdown). Generated: refined standalone constraints with header path and stable hash IDs; JSON file of executable Python checks in four domains: Process (PATH shell shims blocking prohibited commands), Source (Tree-sitter AST queries), Architectural-Deterministic (NetworkX dependency-graph checks), Architectural-Semantic (LLM-as-judge rubrics, warnings only). Violation traces returned to the agent

Check generation: Markdown AST parse -> path-aware slicing -> LLM refinement of each constraint (gpt-5.2-chat) -> intent router to domain -> expert generators (Claude Code + Opus 4.5) with self-test loop, syntax check and dry run -> JSON of checks. Runtime enforcement: shims intercept commands; static/architectural checks on repo, diff or unstaged changes; violations fed back to the agent for self-correction (max 5 rounds in evaluation). Incremental re-generation when instruction file changes
Developers can review and edit the generated JSON checks before deployment; semantic warnings flagged for human review; false positives resolved by refining the instruction file or marking exceptions
Full workflow of the proposed tool (check generation + runtime enforcement) with generated AGENTS.md files

Criterion: SWE-bench Lite tests (resolution) and executable constraint oracle (compliance). All with OpenCode + GPT-5.2 (critic for LLM Reflection: Claude Opus 4.5)
- Vanilla (AGENTS.md in context, no feedback) + OpenCode + GPT-5.2: resolved 159/300 (53.0%); compliance 201 (67.0%); end-to-end mean 327.9 s. Baseline
- LLM Reflection + OpenCode + GPT-5.2 (critic Claude Opus 4.5): resolved 157 (52.3%); compliance 151 (50.3%); avg rounds 2.30, 85 hit cap (28%); feedback 19,455 chars, 133.7 s. Quality: does not work; cost: does not work
- ContextCov + OpenCode + GPT-5.2: resolved 172 (57.3%); compliance 265 (88.3%); avg rounds 1.31, 29 hit cap (10%); feedback 6,292 chars, 27.7 s; end-to-end 422.4 s. Quality: works; cost: works vs LLM Reflection, partly vs Vanilla (end-to-end time higher)

Tasks: SWE-bench Lite (300), with AGENTS.md files generated by a few-shot LLM from existing repo docs, lint configs and CI files. Configurations: Vanilla, LLM Reflection, ContextCov. Baselines: Vanilla and LLM Reflection. Held constant: agent scaffold (OpenCode), coding model (GPT-5.2), instruction files, 5-round feedback budget for both feedback methods. Acceptance tests: official SWE-bench harness; compliance via ContextCov's own oracle (post-hoc for baselines). Repetitions: Not stated (one run per task apparently). Human intervention: none during runs

ContextCov best: resolution 57.3% vs 53.0% Vanilla (+4.3 pts, McNemar p=0.031; discordant 22/9) and 52.3% LLM Reflection (+5.0, p=0.046); Vanilla vs LLM Reflection n.s. (p=0.885). Compliance 88.3% vs 67.0% vs 50.3%. Feedback cost ~3x lower and latency ~80% lower than LLM Reflection; 3.4x higher cost-efficiency. Residual ContextCov violations only source-level

Distinguished the configurations on resolution and compliance. Repeatability: code and results released; single run, no multiplicity correction (stated). Limitations: compliance measured with ContextCov's own checks (oracle favours the approach); generated instruction files may not match maintainer intent; single LLM judge; 12 Python-heavy repos

False positives from LLM misinterpretation, overly strict checks or implicit exceptions; generated instruction files may not match maintainer intent; single LLM-judge configuration; SWE-bench Lite only (12 Python-heavy repos, 300 tasks); subgroup analyses underpowered; McNemar tests without multiplicity correction; replication on other benchmarks needed
